power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Moving objects frequently become occluded from view, yet we often experience a compelling sense of their continued motion and position during occlusion.
Despite this subjective impression, recent behavioral and neuroimaging evidence suggests that representations of moving objects during occlusion may be limited.

Here, across four experiments, we investigated 1) the accuracy of object localization during dynamic occlusion, 2) the motion information which may support successful position judgments, and 3) the relationship between gaze behavior and localization performance.
In Experiment 1a, participants estimated the position of a moving object at unpredictable time points during occlusion.
Position estimates were highly inaccurate, with errors increasing as objects travelled further behind the occluder.
Increasing object speed exacerbated these errors in Experiment 1b, whereas decreasing speed improved performance.
With decreased speed, there was also an increase in pre-occlusion motion information, which may aid object localization during dynamic occlusion.
In Experiment 2, we found post-occlusion motion information could support accurate judgments of object reappearance.

The necessity of post-occlusion information was further supported in Experiment 3, when removing postocclusion motion information while testing a predictable intercept location resulted in inaccurate estimations.
Across experiments, gaze position predicted behavioral errors, with eye movement strategies varying according to task demands.
Together, these findings suggest that the position of moving objects is poorly represented during dynamic occlusion, despite our compelling subjective experience of their occluded location.
Instead, accurate judgments depend critically on information acquired after the object re-emerges, consistent with a postdictive reconstruction of occluded object position.
Moving objects in everyday life often become occluded from sight for varying lengths of time.
For example, vehicles travelling on a highway can often become fully obscured by other vehicles.
Yet, drivers claim to have a strong sensation of the location of occluded vehicles.

This claim has been supported by seminal work on motion perception during occlusion (e.g. Burke, 1952; Michotte, Thinès, & Crabbé, 1964 / Thinès, Costall, & Butterworth,1991; Scholl & Pylyshyn, 1999), although more recent findings have questioned the robustness of occluded motion representation (e.g. Makin & Poliakoff, 2011; Battaglini et al., 2013; Teichmann et al., 2022).

text.text: Here, we tested the reliability of the perceived experience regarding an object's physical position during a period of dynamic occlusion events.

We examine what elements of occluded motion support successful prediction of an occluded object's position and how gaze position during occlusion provides an account of strategy during each occlusion task.

Support for maintained perception of an occluded object has come from tasks requiring estimation of a moving objects' reappearance time following occlusion. Rosenbaum (1975) employed a "prediction-of-motion" task to measure the time-to-contact of an occluded moving object with the end of an occluder.

text.text: With a growing consensus that the representation of an occluded object is weak, how do we reconcile our successful navigation in a world with continually occluded moving items?
Here we aim to understand what elements of occlusion bring about successful position estimates during occlusion.
In Experiments 1a and 1b, we developed a paradigm which probes the inherent representation of object position during occlusion at unpredictable time-points.

The approach to study dynamic position perception at unpredictable locations during occlusion has rarely been employed in previous research, yet it provides clear insight to object localization throughout occlusion without reliance on post-occlusion information provided in interruption paradigms or a predetermined test location found in the typical time-to-contact studies.
In Experiment 1a we found position estimates throughout occlusion were inaccurate, with error increasing as a function of the distance travelled behind the occluder.
In Experiment 1b, we tested whether reducing occlusion duration by increasing object speed would improve position estimates.
Contrary to this prediction, increasing object speed exacerbated position error, whereas decreasing speed improved position estimates.

Decreasing object speed also increased the duration for which the object was visible prior to occlusion, potentially providing additional information that could support position estimation during occlusion.
Thus, Experiments 1a and 1b both demonstrated poor position estimation during occlusion, although errors were reduced at slower object speeds.
In Experiment 2, we examined whether position estimates improved when post-occlusion motion information was available.
With access to post-occlusion information, participants estimated the object's reappearance with high accuracy.
Finally, in Experiment 3, we tested whether post-occlusion information itself was necessary for accurate position estimation, or whether knowledge of a fixed interception location was sufficient.
Participants were therefore asked to determine when the occluded target reached the end of the occluder, eliminating postocclusion motion information while providing a known interception location.
Despite knowledge of this location, position estimates remained inaccurate.
Across all experiments, we additionally found that final gaze position predicted errors in the behavioral localization of the occluded object.
Gaze position during occlusion was heavily influenced by the task, with participants employing different strategies depending on task goals.
Together, these experiments indicate that the position of a moving object is represented inaccurately throughout occlusion.

Accurate estimates of its position during occlusion emerged only when post-occlusion motion information was available, suggesting that perceived object position during occlusion is reconstructed postdictively using information obtained after the object re-emerges.

Second, to identify eyeblinks, we checked how much pupil dilation changed from one timepoint to the next and excluded samples where the pupil dilation change exceeded a threshold based on the participants' data.

text.text: In this task, the target moved at 10.04 degrees/second and was associated with a constant sound (middle C, 261.33 Hz).

After the target became occluded, the target stopped moving at one of seven positions, indicated by the stopping of the sound [97.87, 215.31, 332.76, 450.2, 567.65, 685.09, 802.54 ms, relative to start of occlusion].
Participants completed 167 trials (24 per stopping location), presented in a random order.
The cursor appeared after the sound stopped to the right of the occluder.
Participants were asked to click on the position where they estimated the target to have stopped moving.
No feedback was provided to the participants.
We collapsed across the movement directions and measured how far the estimated stopping position deviated from the true stopping position along the x-axis.

Our subjective impression that we can accurately estimate the position of a moving target during occlusion appears to depend on motion information available after the target re-emerges.
When observers are instead probed to report the target's position while it remains occluded, position estimates are poor.
Across four experiments, our findings suggest that the compelling impression of a continuously represented occluded trajectory may arise through postdiction.
Motion information available after occlusion is integrated retrospectively to reconstruct the target's trajectory during the period in which it was hidden.
Our two experiments which tested dynamic object localization during occlusion demonstrated poor position estimates.
The target was perceived to be moving slower than the reality, resulting in an underestimation of the distance the target travelled behind the occluder.
This underestimation increased with distance travelled under the occluder.
However, when probing target localization across speeds, we found errors increased with faster speeds, indicating shorter durations of occlusion did not improve the position estimate.
Slower targets may be better represented during occlusion due to increased visibility of the dynamic stimulus prior to occlusion (Battaglini & Ghiani, 2021; Teichmann, Edwards, & Baker, 2021).
text.formatted: Slower targets may be better represented during occlusion due to increased visibility of the dynamic stimulus prior to occlusion <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Battaglini & Ghiani, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Teichmann, Edwards, & Baker, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The target in the slowest trials was visible for 1610 ms prior to occlusion compared to 360 ms in the fastest trials.
In both these experiments, gaze fell behind the true target trajectory, reflecting the behavioral signature in the task.

We noted that participants were accurate in position estimation at the first stopping position across all three speeds in Experiment 1b, indicating that target position estimation was close to the true trajectory for a short distance into the occluder.
However, this same effect was not detected in Experiment 1a, indicating that successful position estimation at this stopping location was not reliable.
In our next experiment we found post-occlusion information supported accurate estimation of incorrect target reappearance times.

Participants were accurate at detecting targets which reappeared extremely early or late, and they converged on chance when the target reappeared on time, indicating an equal likelihood of responding "early" or "late".
Eye gaze was also modulated by the task.
Participants followed the target trajectory for ~213 ms during occlusion and then moved ahead of the target.
Therefore, target reappearance improved accuracy and altered the gaze strategy.
Finally, to pinpoint the post-occlusion information as critical for accurate occluded target position estimates, we tested position accuracy with a known probe location (the end of the occluder).
Here participants could use the known intercept location to help estimate the time-to-contact with the end of the occluder, unlike the unpredictable test times studied in experiments 1a and 1b.
However, we found poor estimation of intercept of the moving target with the end of the occluder, and this estimation was worse with faster speeds.
Similar to our first experiments, the target was perceived to move slower than the actual speed.
Finally, eye gaze strategy also supported the task.
Gaze was maintained on the trajectory for ~200 ms, then moved ahead of the occluded stimulus, but then lingered just prior to the end of the occluder.

Another critical element of our final study was the addition of the transparent condition, where participants were estimating the interception of the moving target with the end of the occluder, yet the occluder was transparent.
This condition demonstrates that participants are extremely precise in estimating time-to-contact when the stimulus is visible.
In fact, we can see participants are predicting the interception and factoring in their own reaction time to allow for the precise position estimate.
Some of our findings challenge prevailing interpretations of previous work on dynamic occlusion.
In particular, our results question the assumption that observers maintain an accurate representation of an object's state as it moves behind an occluder.
Instead, our results suggest that post-occlusion motion information may enable a retrospective reconstruction of the object's position during the period of occlusion.

Phenomena such as object persistence has been interpreted across several areas of research as evidence that objects continue to be represented while occluded (Burke, 1952; Michotte, Thinès, & Crabbé, 1964 / Thinès, Costall, & Butterworth,1991; Carey & Xu, 2001; Scholl & Pylyshyn, 1999; Flombaum & Scholl, 2006; Flombaum et al., 2008; Liberman et al., 2016).

text.text: Many of these studies demonstrate that observers tolerate substantial changes to an occluded object provided that a plausible spatiotemporal or kinematic relationship is maintained between the object entering and emerging from the occluder (Flombaum & Scholl, 2006).

text.text: Our findings offer a different interpretation of this tolerance: such changes may be accepted precisely because the representation of the object during occlusion is relatively imprecise, allowing pre-and postocclusion information to interact in determining the perceived state of the object.

Consistent with this account, when a dynamic Gabor changes orientation during occlusion, its post-occlusion orientation is perceived as biased toward its pre-occlusion orientation (Liberman et al., 2016).

text.text: Rather than necessarily demonstrating the maintenance of a detailed representation throughout occlusion, such effects may therefore reflect the retrospective integration of information available before and after occlusion.

Another finding which is questioned in our data is the interpretation that object localization during occlusion is more accurate for shorter durations of occlusion (Lyon & Waag, 1995; Peterken et al., 1991; Bennett et al., 2010; Battaglini et al., 2013).

text.text: Our two experiments which modulated speed demonstrated that shorter durations of occlusion caused by faster moving targets actually increase position error.
Importantly, it was plausible to examine differing occlusion durations due to the different speeds of targets, we did not isolate occlusion duration alone.
Therefore, while occlusion duration was modulated by speed, so was the extent of exposure prior to occlusion.
Longer exposure duration prior to occlusion has been demonstrated to improve position estimates during occlusion (Battaglini & Ghiani, 2021).

text.text: What is clear from our study is that prior exposure eclipses occlusion duration in modulating localization accuracy during occlusion within our experimental parameters.
Our result which demonstrated successful position estimation of a dynamic occluded target was found using an interruption paradigm.

In trials where a moving target reappeared on time after occlusion, we found participants were equally likely to select "too early" or "too late" suggesting this was the point of subjective equality (PSE).
This result replicates that of Battaglini et al., (2013) who also found the PSE at 50% across three occluder lengths for the on-time trials.

text.text: However, studies using interruption paradigms with different judgment tasks have found that participants are relatively poor at explicitly identifying trials in which a target reappears at the correct time (DeLucia & Liddell, 1998; Makin et al., 2008; Makin & Poliakoff, 2011).
text.formatted: However, studies using interruption paradigms with different judgment tasks have found that participants are relatively poor at explicitly identifying trials in which a target reappears at the correct time <ref type="bibr">(DeLucia & Liddell, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Makin et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Makin & Poliakoff, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Why, does performance deteriorate when observers are directly asked to judge whether a reappearance is correctly timed?

Often these prior studies aim manipulate many factors simultaneously within their interruption paradigms including reappearance interval, target speed, and occluder size (DeLucia & Liddell, 1998; Makin et al., 2008; Makin & Poliakoff, 2011).

text.text: The interaction of these factors could influence participants ability to decern a correct reappearance.
Our task also takes a more orthogonal approach by measuring the sensitivity of incorrect target reappearance times.
Our study provides a detailed characterization of gaze patterns during occlusion across multiple dynamic object localization tasks.
Importantly, participants were given no instructions regarding their eye-movements.
They naturally performed the gaze patterns found within each of our four experiments.
Across experiments we found participants gaze mirrored their behavior tightly.
We also found that the task influenced the gaze patterns during occlusion.
When the task focused on unpredictable localization during occlusion, gaze fell behind the occluded moving target.

However, when the task focused on the end of the occluder in either the interruption paradigm or the time-to-contact paradigm, gaze followed the moving target for ~200 ms and then moved ahead of the target.

If the task was regarding reappearance, gaze reached the end of the occluder, however when the task focused on the interception with the end of the occluder, gaze lingered just before the end of the occluder.

The pursuit of the dynamic object into the occluder for ~200ms calls back to the neuroimaging work which has demonstrated position decoding up to ~200ms after occlusion onset (Teichmann et al., 2022; Patel et al., PsyArXiv).

text.text: Perhaps the short period of pursuit into the occluder reflects the neural mechanism detected using MEG and EEG.
This short period of pursuit is also reflected in previous literature on ocular pursuit during occlusion (Orban de Xivry et al., 2005; Bennett & Barnes, 2006).

text.text: Others have also demonstrated an advantage in occluded target localization during free viewing in comparison to fixation tasks (Makin & Poliakoff, 2011).
text.formatted: Others have also demonstrated an advantage in occluded target localization during free viewing in comparison to fixation tasks <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Makin & Poliakoff, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Collectively, evidence across four experiments suggests that position estimates for dynamically occluded objects are poor.

Accurate position estimates emerged only when post-occlusion information was available, suggesting that our apparent ability to localize moving objects during occlusion may rely largely on retrospective processing.
One possibility is that the subjective impression of successful localization is itself supported by this retrospective reconstruction.
In everyday environments, observers rarely need to estimate the position of an occluded moving object with high spatial or temporal precision.
Instead, behavior typically incorporates substantial safety margins that may allow imprecise representations during occlusion to go unnoticed.

For example, when driving, people generally maintain sufficient distance from other vehicles to avoid collisions, meaning that errors in estimating an occluded object's position or time-to-contact may have little consequence and therefore remain undetected.
